A tropical fruit plant native to the tropical Americas, probably southern Mexico and adjacent Central America. Its usually single trunk bears large, deeply lobed leaves near the top, while hard green berries mature into yellow fruit with soft orange flesh. Papayas are eaten fresh, in salads and juices; before ripening, the skin’s milky latex should be removed because it harms mucous membranes.

output.summary: Small creeping flowering plant native to Europe. It has square stems, opposite blunt-toothed leaves and tiny flowers surrounded by bright yellow-green leafy bracts, typically in damp, shady woodland or beside streams.

Spring-flowering bulbous perennial native to the western Iberian Peninsula, excluding the far northwest. Compared with the common bluebell, it has larger, paler and less drooping flowers, broader leaves, blue anthers and little or no scent; pink- and white-flowered forms also occur.

Bushy shrub or spreading tree native to south-eastern Australia. It has bluish-grey or silvery leaves and spherical heads of yellow flowers. Its leaves are sometimes used in Indian chutney, while Ngunnawal and Wiradjuri people traditionally made flour from the seeds.

output.summary: Annual flowering herb native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its leaves have several pairs of narrow leaflets, and it bears solitary flowers or clusters of up to three with yellow or purple-tinged petals.

Fast-growing shrub or small tree endemic to eastern Australia. It has pale green, narrowly oval leaves and white to pale-yellow flower clusters; its egg-shaped fruits are covered with black, blister-like warts.
Flowering plant endemic to Madeira, Portugal. It is protected under Portuguese or European legislation, including the Habitats Directive and the Convention on European Wildlife and Natural Habitats.

Flowering plant native to European mountains from east-central Spain and southern Italy through the Alps and Balkans to the eastern Carpathians. In mainland Portugal, 2016–2019 assessments classified it as Critically Endangered; one recently rediscovered known site may hold fewer than 50 mature plants, following historical records from at least three additional Gerês sites.

Aquatic perennial native to Eurasia, Africa, the Middle East and Australia. Its submerged leaves have conspicuously toothed margins and usually wavy edges, though the waves may be unclear on new growth. It produces overwintering shoots from hardened buds called turions.

Perennial flowering herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its lobed, blue-green leaves release yellow-orange latex when injured, and it bears four-petalled yellow flowers. The whole plant is toxic in moderate doses, and ingestion may damage the liver.
output.edibilityNote: The whole plant is toxic in moderate doses; ingestion may cause liver toxicity.

output.summary: An annual vine native to Southern Africa, the horned melon bears spiny fruit with orange skin and soft, lime-green flesh when ripe. A traditional African food, the fruit may be eaten at any ripeness and is mainly served as a snack or salad in northern Zimbabwe.
output.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten at any ripeness, mainly as a snack or salad in northern Zimbabwe; some people also eat the peel.

output.summary: A perennial herb native to western, central and southern Europe, northwestern Africa, southwestern Western Asia and Siberia, salad burnet has fern-like toothed leaves and crimson spherical flower clusters. Its young leaves, which taste mildly of cucumber, are used in salads, sauces, drinks and flavourings; older leaves become bitter.
output.edibilityNote: Young leaves are used in salads, dressings, sauces, drinks and flavourings; older leaves tend to become bitter.

output.summary: An aquatic perennial native to northern and eastern Australia, and possibly New Guinea, the blue waterlily has large floating leaves and blue or lilac flowers that fade almost white. output.edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians ate roasted tubers, raw peeled stalks and flower buds, and seeds roasted or pounded into flour.

output.summary: A liverwort recorded across Europe, parts of Asia, North Africa, Madeira and North America, cliff scalewort grows mainly in damp, shady mountain habitats. A deciduous tree native to cool temperate Europe and Asia, European aspen has nearly round, coarsely toothed adult leaves that tremble on flattened stalks. It spreads extensively through root sprouts, forming large clonal colonies.
A knapweed native to southwestern Europe and northern Africa.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.

A poisonous perennial herb native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa around the Mediterranean, the villous deadly carrot has hairy, divided leaves and bright yellow flower clusters. Its fruits have four wings, while its thick root resembles a white carrot or turnip.
output.edibilityNote: The plant is described as highly poisonous; its roots can also cause severe itching and swelling on skin contact.

output.summary: A perennial flowering herb native to Eurasia, lesser stitchwort has weak, four-angled stems and narrow leaves. Each white petal is so deeply divided that it appears to be two petals.

A herbaceous perennial in the bedstraw and coffee family. Tiny hooks on its leaves and stems let it climb. Its long roots, harvested after two years, have supplied red textile dyes since ancient times.
output.edibilityNote: Root-derived dyes have been used as food ingredients.

output.summary: A cycad native to the Lebombo Mountains of Mozambique, Eswatini and South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal province. It commonly forms clumps from basal shoots and has stiff leaves with glossy dark-green leaflets. Male and female cones grow on separate plants, and its seeds have bright red outer coats.

A flowering plant in the carnation family, native in countries from the Mediterranean to northern Somalia and Pakistan. It is listed as invasive in Australia and France, occurring particularly in drier parts of southeastern Australia.
A bulb-growing plant native from southern Europe to northern Iraq. It produces bluish-purple flowers in March and April on tall flowering stalks.

A large deciduous tree native to much of Europe, especially humid climates. Young trees and clipped hedges often retain their dead leaves until spring. Its nuts are eaten, although large quantities are slightly toxic; historically they were pressed for cooking oil or soaked before being ground into flour.
output.edibilityNote: Nuts are eaten but are slightly toxic in large quantities; they were used for cooking oil or soaked to remove tannins before making flour.

output.summary: A sedge native to parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia. It grows in wet places such as river margins and rice fields.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal. It is protected under legislation including Annexes II and IV of the EU Habitats Directive.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It is not protected under Portuguese or EU legislation.

A frost-tender perennial succulent native to Madagascar. It has fleshy blue-green leaves with scalloped edges that may turn pink or red in strong sunlight or drought. Its lax stems often root where they touch the ground, producing new plants.
Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal, it is confined to a few siliceous rocky deposits high in Serra da Estrela and has a very small population.

Flowering succulent with no explicitly stated native origin; it occurs from the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa to Sicily. Its papillate leaves and preference for gypsum and limestone distinguish it.

Erect herb with no explicitly stated native origin, widespread across most of Europe and extending into Morocco, the Caucasus and southwestern Asia. It has almost round leaves in whorls of four and green fruits covered with long hooked hairs.
Flowering plant whose subspecies carpetana is native to mainland Portugal.
Sprawling perennial herb native to Europe. Surface runners form dense mats of purple-tinged leaves, while spring stalks carry many blue or purple flowers.
output.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw, in salads or as tea; only small amounts are advised, and older leaves become more bitter.

output.summary: Perennial climbing herb of uncertain native origin, possibly spanning Cape Verde to the Arabian Peninsula through Africa and the Mediterranean. It has deeply divided leaves, bulbous roots and large white-to-lavender funnel-shaped flowers.
output.edibilityNote: Most parts are reportedly edible; roots are eaten cooked and young leaves are eaten, though ingestion can cause respiratory symptoms.

output.summary: Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
Succulent flowering plant native to Mexico. It has soft, spineless leaves and, after many years, produces an unusually curved, swan-neck-like flower cluster before the flowering rosette dies.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal.
Flowering plant native to Europe and Asia.

Plant endemic to southwestern mainland Portugal, growing in scrub clearings on sandy soils. Its current distribution and population are highly uncertain because it has repeatedly been confused with a close relative; seven locations are identified, and suitable habitat has declined in recent decades.

Deciduous tree native to south-central and southeastern China. Its hanging flower heads are surrounded by two large white bracts that flutter like doves or handkerchiefs, while its hard nuts contain seeds that may take three years to germinate.

Annual grass native to the southern United States, usually found in moist or wet ground and disturbed areas. It has a hairy, roughly oval flower head. Its grains occur at archaeological sites across several states, and it was probably cultivated by pre-Columbian Native Americans.

Annual flowering plant thought to be native to western South America. Its pale violet, bell-shaped flowers open for only a few hours each day, later developing a deeply lobed, lantern-like covering around the fruit. Introduced widely, it commonly occurs as a weed of cultivated and waste ground.
output.edibilityNote: Accounts conflict: cooked tender leaves, berries and processed seed jelly are eaten, but the whole plant and berries have also been described as toxic.

output.summary: Perennial horsetail widespread across cooler Eurasia and North America. Its wind-carried spores bear four long ribbon-like structures, and the plant can also spread through runners.
output.edibilityNote: Some sources consider it safe in moderate amounts when properly cooked, although it is poisonous to mammals and heat may denature its thiaminases.

output.summary: Perennial nettle found in Japan, China and Taiwan, where it inhabits moist mountain forests. Its stinging hairs can cause pain, redness, burning or itching. After boiling to destroy its toxicity, it is used in Taiwan in soup, bread, shortbread and fried leaves.
output.edibilityNote: Boiling destroys its toxicity; Taiwanese uses include soup, bread, Chinese shortbread and crispy fried leaves.

output.summary: Plant endemic to Mexico, but introduced to Florida, Central and South America, the West Indies and several Pacific islands.
Shrub native to the Mediterranean region. It has aromatic foliage and midsummer spikes of lavender flowers, and several ancient Mediterranean cultures used it as a spice.

output.summary: Tree native to the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States, Mexico's Yucatán coast, Bermuda and parts of the Caribbean. Its trunk bears sharp, strap-like leaves and eventually topples before its tip turns upward and continues growing. Humans eat the fruit and the showy white flowers, which may be eaten raw or cooked.

output.summary: Coastal plant endemic to southwestern mainland Portugal, growing on consolidated sandy cliff soils with some iron and surface moisture. In the 2016–2019 assessment, only three subpopulations were known, two created by reintroduction at historical sites, while habitat and population declines continued.
Small shrub of unknown origin, distributed in Asia and Mexico. Its terminal flower clusters are yellow with red at the base, and it grows beside streams in mountain, oak and pine forests.
Evergreen tree native to eastern and southern Asia. New leaves are deep purple-crimson before becoming glossy green above and blue-green below, while its acorn cups have distinctive concentric rings.
output.edibilityNote: Acorns are edible; dried, ground acorns can be mixed with cereals as flour, and roasted seeds can substitute for coffee.

output.summary: Wild grass originating in tropical Asia. It is the wild ancestor of sawa millet, although some taxonomists combine the wild and domesticated forms. In India, its seeds are prepared as khichdi and eaten during festival fasting days.
output.edibilityNote: In India, seeds are cooked as khichdi for festival fasts; historically in Australia, seeds were pounded, mixed with water and made into bread.

output.summary: Tree native to southern Africa, with an isolated population in eastern Zimbabwe. It bears abundant sprays of bright yellow flowers and thin, papery, straw-coloured pods.
Flowering plant endemic to mainland Portugal. It is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

Wildflower native to the New World, occurring widely in Mexico and parts of the southwestern United States. It resembles a dandelion but has white-to-pink flowers, with reports that white blooms become pinkish as they age. Injured parts release white latex, and its stems bear a few leaves.

Annual flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its wild form is hairy and glandular, with intricately divided, lacy leaves and coiling clusters of blue or lavender flowers. Its seeds germinate only in darkness.
Tufted annual grass native to Europe, Asia and northern Africa, and widely naturalised elsewhere. It has green flowers and curved growth reflected in several of its common names.

A densely foliaged shrub or small tree native to Australia, moonah has rough dark bark and a trunk often twisted by wind. Its white or cream flower spikes appear mainly in summer, followed by woody capsules spaced along the branches.

A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Europe and North Africa, creeping velvet grass grows in woods and hedgerows. Disturbed rhizome fragments can produce fresh shoots, and its hairy stem joints help distinguish it from similar grass.
A succulent shrub whose native origin is not stated, orange dewplant has a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves.

An upright perennial herb native to northern parts of the Northern Hemisphere, marsh skullcap grows beside fens and shorelines. Its blue flowers occur in pairs along one side of the stem rather than at the top.

An upright evergreen shrub native to Madeira and the central and western Canary Islands, this plant has slender branches and narrow to broad lance-shaped leaves. Its pale powder-blue or whitish flower heads are dense, rounded and usually crowded near the stem tips.

A massive, long-lived tree native to the eastern and central United States, northeastern Mexico and extreme southern Canada, the American sycamore favours wetlands and riversides. Its bark flakes away in large irregular pieces, creating a mottled surface of gray, greenish-white and brown.

An evergreen or semi-evergreen ground fern native to New Zealand, the Chatham Islands, several New Zealand subantarctic islands and Australia’s Macquarie Island, prickly shield fern has an erect, scaly underground stem that may form a short trunk. Round spore clusters occur beneath its fronds.

A slow-growing evergreen conifer endemic to Japan, koyamaki has reddish-brown bark that peels in vertical strips. Its glossy dark green, needle-like modified stems form distinctive umbrella-shaped clusters at the branch ends, while its seed cones take about two years to mature.

An evergreen tree of unstated native origin, Natal mahogany is found from South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal Province to tropical Africa. It has glossy dark green leaves, a wide crown and sweet-scented flowers; its black seeds are almost enclosed by bright red coverings, and its fruit is emetic.

output.summary: A rainforest plant native to South America, Aztec tobacco is exceptionally potent, with leaves containing up to nine times more nicotine than common tobacco. Its nicotine-rich leaves are used to produce pesticides and in varied cultural preparations.
output.edibilityNote: In Peru it is drunk as juice for entheogenic purposes; no human food use is documented.

output.summary: Annual climbing herb native to southern Europe, North Africa and nearby islands. Dense stem hairs can give it a silvery-white appearance, while one-sided flower clusters bear dark reddish-purple blooms.
output.edibilityNote: Seeds and forage have been reported to poison humans.

output.summary: Flowering plant native to the Canary Islands and Mediterranean shores. In Portugal it occurs in sometimes disturbed coastal habitats with some salinity, and it is used in research intended to improve sugar beet.

Fern native to much of temperate Europe, Asia and North America. Its upright, semi-evergreen leaves form a single crown, with orange-brown scales on their stalks; mature leaves release spores from August to November.
output.edibilityNote: The rhizomes are toxic; excessive doses can cause serious poisoning, blindness or death.

output.summary: True ginger native to Maritime Southeast Asia. Its beehive-like flower spikes have white, yellow, orange or red bracts that often darken as they mature, surrounding small purple-and-yellow flowers with a papery texture.
Herbaceous perennial; many varieties introduced to North America are native to Europe and Western Asia. It bears spikes of lilac-to-purple flowers and opposite, dark green, lance-shaped leaves.
Plant found in France and northern Italy.

Evergreen or partly deciduous climber native to southern Brazil, Bolivia, northeastern Argentina and Paraguay. Dense clusters of orange flowers appear from winter to spring, while forked tendrils cling to rough surfaces such as brick walls.
Annual or perennial herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its slender glandular stems carry slightly fleshy, threadlike leaves, sometimes with hard or spiny tips, and small pink flowers.

Subtropical succulent tree native to Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Its thick branches bear clusters of sharp spines and fleshy leaves, with reddish flower-like structures grouped near the branch ends.

Willow shrub or small tree native to much of temperate Canada and the United States. It has dark, scaly bark and thick leaves that are hairy underneath; silky catkins emerge before the leaves in early spring.

A flowering shrub endemic to southern California, Nevin's barberry has dense evergreen foliage of dark green to bluish-green, spiny-toothed leaflets. Its bright yellow flowers appear in spring, followed by reddish summer berries that eventually turn dark blue.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to woodlands of the southeastern United States, oakleaf hydrangea has large lobed leaves with silvery-white undersides that turn red, bronze and purple in autumn. Its upright, cone-shaped flower clusters open white and age to pink or brown, depending on the cultivar or seedling.

A low-growing evergreen conifer shrub native to Japan, Japanese garden juniper spreads through long branches that intertwine into a dense mat. Its needle-like leaves grow in threes, and female plants bear dark, berry-like cones with a pale blue-white coating.
A perennial flowering herb native to most of Europe except Ireland, Iceland and the Greek islands, and also native to parts of western and central Asia, wild liquorice is sometimes used to make tea.

output.summary: A flowering thistle endemic to mainland Portugal, Cirsium welwitschii is restricted to the subcoastal belt between Baixo Vouga and southwestern Alentejo, chiefly on permanently waterlogged ground. Its stem leaves are often poorly developed or absent, while its basal leaves are comparatively well developed. It is rare, with widely separated populations that are usually very small.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and the Azores.

A prostrate flowering succulent endemic to eastern Australia, angular sea-fig usually grows very close to the sea. It has blue-grey leaves, daisy-like light-purple to deep pinkish-purple flowers, and red to purple fruit that ripens mainly in summer and autumn.
output.edibilityNote: Aboriginal peoples ate the fruit; the fleshy leaves may be eaten raw or cooked, and roasted leaves can serve as a salt substitute.

output.summary: A flowering plant native to central and southern Europe.

A low-growing herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia, white clover forms spreading mats as its creeping stems root at the nodes. Its leaves almost always have three leaflets, while the whitish flower heads may become tinged pink or cream as they age.
output.edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are survival food; raw plants are hard to digest, but boiling helps. Avoid flowers long after picking because cyanides may form.

output.summary: A perennial wetland herb native across most of Eurasia and locally in northwestern Africa, narrow-leaved cattail grows in fresh or brackish water. Its slender leaves overtop the flowering stem, whose upper male and lower female sections are separated by a conspicuous bare gap; the female section matures into a rusty-brown, sausage-shaped spike.
output.edibilityNote: Depending on season, edible parts include dormant root and leaf-base sprouts, stalk cores, green flower spikes, ripe pollen and starchy roots; prepare like broadleaf cattail.

output.summary: A small, clump-forming plant endemic to South Africa’s Eastern Cape, it has rosettes of thick, light-green leaves. Its soft, boat-shaped leaves usually have transparent streaks near their tips, which may be the only parts visible above the sand in the wild.
A perennial flowering plant native to the forest understorey of Asia, it has long, pointed leaves and strongly scented white flowers with yellow bases. Its flower buds and young flowers are edible.

output.summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it is introduced in the Azores and Madeira.

A perennial grass native to Asia and Australia, it forms graceful, spreading clumps. Its narrow green leaves turn golden yellow and then beige, while arching, brush-like flower spikes change from silvery or pinkish white to brown as seeds form.
A plant native to Madagascar and Europa Island in the Mozambique Channel, it inhabits dry forests, dry shrubland and rocky areas. It is threatened by habitat loss.

A subtropical, succulent-leaved plant endemic to the Canary Islands except Lanzarote, it also occurs as a subspontaneous plant in Portugal’s Serra de Sintra. It has woolly growth and soft leaves whose margins are widest near the base.

An aquatic plant whose native origin is not supplied, it forms dense mats along pond margins and can outcompete other plants. It produces viable seeds but also reproduces very effectively through vegetative growth, while its large, showy flowers attract many kinds of insects.

A liverwort possibly originating in Southeast Asia, it is now widely distributed across temperate Northern Hemisphere regions. Its highly divided leaves give its loose, pale-green to yellowish-white mats a feathery or fuzzy appearance, especially in moist, shaded places near springs and streams.
A plant native to Venezuela, Trinidad and Tobago, and the Netherlands Antilles.

An upright, spineless shrub from the Mediterranean region, it has young branches tipped with white hairs and leaves divided into three leaflets. Its yellow flowers appear from late winter through spring and sometimes into summer, followed by pods covered in whitish hairs.

A large deciduous tree common on the plains and lower hills of South and Southeast Asia. Its leaves crowd toward branch tips, and its rounded nuts have five flatter sides. The kernels are eaten by the Lodha people of the Indian subcontinent for their mind-altering qualities.

output.summary: A daisy native to western Europe, Algeria, Morocco and Spain. Unlike the similar Bellis sylvestris, its seeds have scales on the pappus.

A bulbous perennial native to South Africa's Northern and Western Cape Provinces. In late summer and early autumn, it produces clusters of scarlet, lily-like flowers with conspicuous stamens and purple anthers. Its cut flowers are notably long-lasting.

A deciduous shrub native to Taiwan, Vietnam and most of mainland China. It bears rounded clusters of fragrant rose, crimson or pink flowers in late summer, while its crushed leaves smell unpleasant. Its rapid suckering growth can form spreading colonies.
A flowering plant whose nominate subspecies, Linaria viscosa subsp. viscosa, is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and occurs in mainland Portugal.
A flowering plant native to China, the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. Compounds extracted from its dried leaves and stems have shown activity against one malaria parasite.
A moss common in Britain. It forms creeping mats on decaying tree stumps, hedgebanks and other shaded places, and can also live underwater.
A daffodil native to Spain, Portugal and Morocco. It has solitary yellow flowers that range from horizontal to upright and grows on rocky cliffs, dunes and meadows in either lime-rich or acidic soil.
A flowering plant endemic to the Azores, where it occurs on four of the nine islands. It grows in upland meadows, shrubland, cliffs, slopes, woods and roadsides.
An evergreen shrub endemic to China. It bears sweet-scented yellow flowers and purple-blue berries that are acidic, seedy and edible raw or cooked.

output.summary: An annual, self-supporting herb with broad leaves, Ononis mitissima is notably tiny, reaching only about five centimetres tall.
A flowering plant native to Southern Africa, Ceropegia linearis has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

An erect perennial herb widespread across much of North America, western ragweed also grows as an introduced plant elsewhere. Its hairy stems bear deeply divided leaves and flower spikes, while a creeping root system allows it to sprout as well as reproduce by seed.
An annual, self-supporting herb, Silene nocturna has simple broad leaves and remains under about forty centimetres tall.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, Echinops strigosus belongs to the daisy family.
A flowering plant, Herniaria scabrida has listed varieties found in mainland Portugal and described as native only to the Iberian Peninsula.

A perennial herb native to the Americas from Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina and Chile, seashore vervain has become introduced worldwide and is sometimes a noxious weed. Its rough, serrated leaves accompany upright spikes of small purple tubular flowers.

A woody plant native to mainland Portugal, Madeira and the Azores, sea knotgrass is usually prostrate, with thick, twisted stems and lance-shaped leaves. A 1913 Portuguese flora describes it as frequent on coastal sands and present in flower almost all year.

A ground-growing orchid native to Central America and northern South America, the fire-star orchid produces long fleshy roots along most of its stem. Its showy red-orange flowers can appear throughout the year and have a tiny cross-shaped central lip.

A small evergreen shrub native to Madeira, Bystropogon punctatus is rare there and grows mainly along edges and clearings of laurel forest. Its branching stems bear aromatic, usually serrated leaves and small flowers ranging from white to purplish violet.
